title: The two-step swap
description:
When you call a function without a namespace in front, the compiler also searches the namespaces of the **argument types**. That is *argument-dependent lookup* (ADL), and it is why `std::cout << x` finds an `operator<<` that lives in `std`.

It matters for `swap`. A type can supply its own, faster `swap` in its own namespace. Writing `std::swap(a, b)` skips it. Writing plain `swap(a, b)` finds it, but then fails for `int`, which has no namespace to search.

The idiom that works for everything has two steps:

```cpp
using std::swap;   // the fallback
swap(a, b);        // unqualified: ADL picks a better one if the type has it
```

Fix `orderTwo` to use it.
hints: Inside your function, write `using std::swap;` and then call plain `swap(a, b);`. For a type with its own `swap` in its namespace, lookup finds that one; for `int`, it uses `std::swap`.
rules: Bring `std::swap` in with a using-declaration, then call `swap` unqualified.
lessonTitle: Name Lookup, ADL, Inline Namespaces and the ODR
